ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

forearm shaft — clinical pattern 3

A patient sustains a radial head fracture after axial loading through the hand. He also has forearm tenderness and wrist pain. Further assessment identifies interosseous membrane disruption and distal radioulnar joint instability, without a radial shaft fracture. Which combined injury is present?

  1. Isolated ulnar shaft fracture
  2. Both-bone forearm shaft fracture
  3. Essex-Lopresti injury
  4. Galeazzi fracture-dislocation
  5. Monteggia fracture-dislocation
Answer and explanation

Essex-Lopresti injury

A radial head fracture is associated with interosseous membrane disruption and distal radioulnar joint injury.

Option explanations

Essex-Lopresti injury: A radial head fracture is associated with interosseous membrane disruption and distal radioulnar joint injury.

Galeazzi fracture-dislocation: A radial shaft fracture is associated with disruption of the distal radioulnar joint. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Monteggia fracture-dislocation: An ulnar fracture or deformity is accompanied by radial head dislocation. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Isolated ulnar shaft fracture: A direct blow may fracture the ulnar shaft without radial fracture or associated proximal or distal joint disruption. This is not the pattern specified in this case.

Both-bone forearm shaft fracture: Fractures of both radial and ulnar shafts can disrupt the alignment required for pronation and supination. This is not the pattern specified in this case.
